name: Engineering vs Physics Barrier
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: We Know It Works. We Don't Know How to Build It.
lesson.summary: The physics of quantum computing is settled and demonstrated at small scale; what remains unsolved is the engineering of manufacturing, wiring, cooling, and controlling that physics reliably at a million-qubit scale.
lesson.body:
It helps to separate two very different kinds of question about quantum computing. One is a physics question: does the underlying idea actually work, does superposition and entanglement really let a device perform certain calculations that classical computers cannot feasibly perform? On that question, the answer for decades now has been a confident yes. Small quantum devices in labs have repeatedly demonstrated entanglement, interference, and, in a growing number of specific benchmark tasks, computations that no known classical computer or algorithm can reproduce in a reasonable time. Decoherence and gate errors are real physical effects that limit how these devices behave, but their behavior is understood well enough to build working, if noisy, quantum processors today.

The other question is an engineering one: given that the physics works, can a device be built, manufactured, wired, cooled, and controlled reliably enough, and at large enough scale, to run the algorithms that would make it economically or scientifically transformative? That question does not have a settled answer, and it is a fundamentally different kind of problem. The decoherence problem and the error rate problem are physical effects that any real qubit will always fight against to some degree, since no physical system is perfectly isolated from its environment. But turning "we can keep one qubit coherent for a fraction of a second in a lab" into "we can keep a million interconnected qubits coherent long enough to run a multi-hour algorithm, manufactured reproducibly, wired without an unmanageable tangle of cables, and cooled without an unmanageable amount of energy" is not a physics problem anymore. It is closer to the kind of problem that separates a working prototype from a mass-produced product.

The history of classical computing offers a genuinely useful comparison here, not as a guarantee that quantum computing will follow the same path, but as an illustration of how large this gap can be. The transistor was demonstrated in 1947, and the physics behind it was well understood almost immediately. It still took decades of manufacturing innovation, in materials science, lithography, and fabrication process control, before transistors could be reliably printed by the billions on a single chip. Nobody doubted the physics of the transistor in 1948. What took decades was the unglamorous work of making that physics manufacturable at scale.

Quantum computing today sits in a comparable position. The open question is not whether qubits can exist and be entangled, that has been settled, but whether any known engineering approach can scale the reliable production, wiring, cooling, and control of qubits from the hundreds seen today to the millions needed for fault tolerance. That is the engineering versus physics barrier, and it is the frame that should be applied to every specific obstacle covered in the rest of this chapter.
